items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## Problem

Successful real research runs still have a large per-case memory footprint for individual users. On current `feat/jiuwenswarm`, the highest observed worker cgroup peak is **11.12 GiB**. Although the latest GraphMemory fix prevented the previously observed runaway behavior in this experiment, this steady operational footprint deserves separate investigation and reduction for ordinary personal computers.

This is a resource-efficiency issue, not a report of another GraphMemory OOM. It is separate from #210 / its fix #212.

## Measured evidence

Experiment revision: `17d0774a` (includes #212 and TC Judge fix #209).

- Nine real scientific E2E cases, three repetitions each; four case workers concurrently.
- GraphMemory enabled throughout, local backend, isolated graph directory per case/repetition.
- Native task dispatch with Swarm execution; generator/Judge `deepseek-flash`.
- Each worker has a 24 GiB cgroup limit and no swap. The group includes the platform stack, graph service, Swarm, Runner and descendants, browser, and Judge.
- All 27 attempts delivered successfully. Retained `memory.events` show `max=0`, `oom=0`, `oom_kill=0` for every worker.

| Case / repetition | Worker cgroup peak (GiB) | Sampled Node API RSS peak (GiB) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| TC-E2E-01 / 1 | 11.124 | 0.977 |
| DRB-75 / 1 | 11.123 | 1.127 |
| DRB-62 / 2 | 10.796 | 0.952 |
| DRB-75 / 3 | 10.397 | 1.275 |
| DRB-59 / 2 | 10.107 | 1.080 |

The three worker peaks for TC-E2E-01 were 11.12 / 8.27 / 8.43 GiB; DRB-75 was 11.12 / 8.61 / 10.40 GiB. Even PUCT's workers peaked around 4.41 GiB in this setup.

**Measurement boundaries:**

- Cgroup peak includes charged file cache and other memory, not just anonymous RSS. It is not proof that the application requires 11 GiB of unreclaimable working memory.
- API RSS is sampled separately and its maximum need not coincide with the group peak. Do not subtract these maxima to infer another component's usage.
- GraphMemory did not appear in the retained high-RSS process samples, but these contain only the host's top 12 processes above a threshold, so its precise individual peak cannot be recovered.
- This harness includes Playwright and diagnostic sampling. Startup/provisioning, browser, diagnostics, page cache, child agents, and runtime costs must be separated before attributing the footprint to the product or GraphMemory.
- Concurrent cases and agent choices varied; this is not a controlled concurrency-scaling measurement.

## Why this matters

Users on 8–16 GiB machines also need memory for the OS, browser, and other applications. Raising per-worker limits or recommending large-memory hosts is not an adequate resource-efficiency strategy. We need to establish the actual working set and provide a practical personal-machine configuration without silently dropping research evidence or quality requirements.

## Investigation and optimization plan

1. Record `memory.stat` (`anon`, `file`, `kernel`, `slab`, etc.), `memory.current/peak/events`, and memory pressure alongside process-tree attribution for the **specific worker cgroup**. Capture phase markers for startup, provisioning, child research, synthesis, and grading.
2. Sample process RSS/PSS by role: API, Swarm/gateway, graph, Runner/executions, browser, Judge. Keep diagnostics lightweight and credential-free; measure profiler overhead explicitly.
3. Reproduce TC-E2E-01 and DRB-75 alone and with concurrent child tasks. Measure the idle stack separately and compare with/without the browser/profiling overhead. Preserve GraphMemory and the same delivery/scoring contract.
4. Identify avoidable duplication or retention only from profiles: repeated runtime processes, scientific environments/imports, per-agent contexts, trajectory buffers, graph state, caches, and teardown. Do not assume any one is the culprit from aggregate peaks.
5. Optimize the dominant confirmed contributors. If required, provide explicit resource-aware concurrency/backpressure and document the latency tradeoff rather than changing research tasks or silently disabling capabilities.

## Acceptance criteria

- Produce a component/phase memory breakdown for the highest-footprint cases, distinguishing reclaimable cache from working memory.
- Establish a measured baseline and a concrete lower memory budget suitable for a representative personal machine, with headroom for OS and interactive use; do not invent a target before attribution.
- Demonstrate improvement against that baseline on the same tasks, with GraphMemory enabled, no OOM, retained artifact delivery, and quality scoring reported independently.
- Check memory release after task completion and repeated use within a long-lived session; include lightweight regression monitoring where practical.

Retained evidence on the experiment host (not publicly accessible):
`/root/sciencediscovery-real9-graph-3x-20260927/case-summary.csv`, plus each case's `memory.csv`, `memory-events.txt`, and `memory-profiles/memory-*.jsonl`.
items.title: [Feature] Reduce real research memory footprint for personal machines: worker peaks reach 11.12 GiB

items.body:
## 背景 / 输入

在 ScienceDiscovery 沙箱 / science-env 中复现 meK-means（Monod `mminference`）：

- 环境：`/opt/science-env/bin/python`
- 依赖：`monod==0.2.9.0`、`loompy`、`anndata`、较新的 `numpy`（≥2）

Case：`s43588-024-00689-2`；驱动脚本 `run.py`。

## 问题是什么

Monod 0.2.9.0 与 **numpy 2** 组合需要额外 shim 才能跑通作者路径，例如：

- `np.meshgrid` 返回值按 list 使用的兼容
- float bounds / `gridsize=[1,1]` 等调用约定修补

否则 Agent 卡在依赖/兼容调试，而不是论文复现本身。预装科学栈「开箱可跑作者代码」的承诺打折。

## 我们怎么规避的

在会话内自建/修补 `mekmeans-cpu` 路径与 shim（详见会话 `REPRODUCTION_REPORT.md` §3），再跑真实 loom。

## 期望应该是什么样

1. science-env（或官方 skill）对常见复现栈给出**钉死且测过的** monod/numpy/loompy 组合，或提供已知 shim 文档。
2. Agent 首次导入失败时，表面友好的「已知兼容问题 + 推荐 pin」提示，而不是长 traceback 试错。
3. 可选：NatureBench / 论文复现模板预装最小可跑镜像，与 brief 中的计算提示对齐。
items.title: [Bug] science-env Monod 0.2.9 × numpy≥2 needs shim for meK-means paper reproduce

items.author: HongyeZhou
items.body:
## Motivation

Long-running offline computations and Agent conversations have different lifecycles. An Agent turn can finish while a training, simulation, or batch-processing task continues running. After evaluation, this is a feature-design topic about coordination between offline tasks and Agents, rather than a defect in turn completion.

This issue replaces #434 and preserves its motivating scenario.

## Motivating scenario

In the NatureBench reproduction session `93f897ca-cefe-4e7b-932d-8339cbef1459`, run `84d71b8a-77dd-42a7-bc81-15e326b14cb1` completed while a background `python run.py --instances mop_sc` computation continued. The final computation took approximately 1,587.7 seconds and produced `predictions.npy` with shape `(5693,)`.

The user had to inspect host processes and wait for the output manually. Starting another Agent run could also launch duplicate work. An Agent promising to return after a wall-clock delay is not a reliable scheduling mechanism.

## Feature scope

Design how long-running offline tasks collaborate with Agents across turns:

- Give supported offline tasks a queryable identity and lifecycle, with ownership linked to the originating session/run.
- Make ongoing computation visible even after the initiating Agent turn finishes.
- Let a later turn inspect, await, or resume coordination with the same task without starting duplicate computation.
- Define how task completion, failure, cancellation, and results become available to the user and Agent.
- Define the default turn-completion policy when a task is still running, including whether explicit detachment is required.
- Document lifecycle limits, including runtime/service restarts and the treatment of processes launched outside the supported task mechanism.

## Design decisions before implementation

- Turn completion: wait for the task, require explicit detach, or register it in the background and notify.
- Ownership and persistence: session-level versus run-level handles, and restart behavior.
- Minimum user interface: how users discover active tasks, inspect progress, and retrieve results.
- Agent continuation: explicit user-driven await/resume versus automatic completion notification or continuation.
- Delivery decomposition: build on existing execution/query/wait capabilities and split implementation into reviewable changes.

These are open design questions; this issue does not select a policy.

## Acceptance criteria

- A user starts a representative long-running computation and can distinguish Agent-turn completion from task completion.
- The same supported task remains discoverable and queryable across turns according to the documented lifecycle.
- The Agent can inspect or await that task and retrieve its final result without launching a duplicate.
- Completion, failure, and cancellation have defined, verifiable user-visible outcomes.
- The chosen turn-completion and restart policies are documented and covered by matching end-to-end scenarios.

## Related work

- #434: original report and evidence; superseded by this feature proposal.
- #439: redirected output buffering. Log buffering is a separate concern; coordinate where progress reporting intersects.
items.title: [Feature] Coordinate long-running offline tasks with Agents across turns

### Background

Follow-up to #96, under the backend migration tracked in #84. This issue carries forward the unfinished scope of #96 for release 0.4.0. Closing #96 is an administrative handover, not a claim that its original acceptance criteria have all passed.

Code review baseline: main at `5a86d0593a887e825d3a3da136f760b62807f797` (2026-10-28). This assessment is based on static inspection, not a fresh full acceptance run.

### Existing behavior to preserve

- Keep the existing Runner and its bwrap / Seatbelt sandbox. Do not switch to jiuwenbox or re-enable JiuwenSwarm host execution/file tools.
- Existing environment, execution and workspace functionality remains available through the legacy API behind the adapter proxy.
- Sandbox network settings already have permission-epoch rotation and persistent-kernel teardown behavior in the legacy API. Preserve and verify it rather than treating it as missing.
- Some L1 contract cases already exist, including sandbox network and package-source settings. The historical claim of 21 uncovered rows must be recalculated against current main.

### Remaining scope

- [ ] Inventory every interface row from #96, including the expanded Runner-specific environment paths. Record its current owner, downstream target, existing coverage and remaining work. Preserve the original interface scope; explicitly justify any row requiring no migration.
- [ ] Complete adapter routing and necessary adaptation for local Runner environments, environment setup/revisions, execution records/status/logs/cancellation, kernel teardown, workspace listing/files/sync/deletion, and local Runner list/detail/connect/probe. Replace reliance on the generic legacy API fallback for this scope with explicit ownership and dispatch; reuse existing implementation where possible instead of rewriting the Runner.
- [ ] Implement the required path rewriting (`/api/environments*` to Runner `/environments*`) and dispatch of `/api/runners/:id/...`, preserving authentication, request/response contracts and errors.
- [ ] Complete `agent-activity` aggregation across Runner executions/transfers, JiuwenSwarm cron/schedules and adapter-owned state, including logs and cancellation. Current main aggregates legacy API stores; that alone does not establish the requested integration.
- [ ] Trace and complete configuration persistence and propagation for sandbox network settings and package-source settings. Verify Runner behavior after saving, permission-epoch rotation and invalidation of previous sandbox authorization where required by #96; preserve existing kernel teardown behavior. Explicitly document the intended epoch behavior for package-source changes and resolve any discrepancy with #91/#96.
- [ ] Evaluate whether the `agent-activity` wrapper can be eliminated; record the conclusion and retain only necessary adaptation.

### Boundaries and dependencies

Local Runner environments, execution and workspace only. Remote-host and NPU implementation remains in #104. Coordinate shared routing/dispatch contracts with that issue without absorbing its scope. Adapter core and settings contracts relate to #87 and #91; downstream consumers include #97 and #102.

The sandbox choice is already settled: retain Runner execution and bwrap / Seatbelt.

### Acceptance

- [ ] Publish a current interface-by-interface coverage matrix for all rows inherited from #96. Each row has an L1 contract diff case or an explicit, justified "no migration needed" classification. Include write operations such as connect, probe, install, uninstall and delete, not just reads.
- [ ] Relevant execution/activity/cancellation and settings-related events have L2 golden traces, with intentional differences documented.
- [ ] Register and run E2E journeys covering environment creation and dependency installation/uninstallation, execution status/logs/cancellation, kernel teardown, workspace inspection/cleanup, and aggregated activity/timer cancellation on the JiuwenSwarm stack.
- [ ] Verify sandbox network-policy changes reach actual Runner execution, out-of-allowlist access is refused, epoch changes do not reuse previous sandbox authorization, and package-source changes affect subsequent package operations. Apply the baseline/assertion and security-case review rules from #84.
- [ ] Demonstrate that the scoped routes use the intended explicit routing/ownership rather than silently succeeding through the generic legacy fallback.
- [ ] Record the wrapper decision, candidate SHA, executed test results and any remaining gaps. Do not mark complete while inherited acceptance items remain uncovered, failed, blocked or skipped.

- Current settings and activity handlers: `services/api/src/http/index.ts`

items.body:
## 背景 / 输入

长 EM 任务 `mop_sc`（约 26.5 min）通过重定向写入 `logs/mop_sc.log`。进程全程 ~100% CPU，但日志在 gene select 附近长时间停在很小体积（约 623 B），直到进程退出才刷出大量内容。

## 问题是什么

Python/`print` **块缓冲**（非 TTY）导致：

- 用户与监控误判「卡住」
- Agent 更容易用墙钟定时器提前结束 turn（加剧孤儿作业问题）

## 我们怎么规避的

不以日志增长为唯一心跳；改看 `ps` CPU、RSS、以及最终 `predictions.npy` 是否落盘。事后用 `[TIMED]` 行核对 wall/cpu/RSS。

## 期望应该是什么样

1. 产品拉起的长时间命令默认 `python -u` / `PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1`，或对重定向日志做行缓冲。
2. Session/job UI 提供进程级心跳（CPU、RSS、最近输出时间），不单靠日志文件 mtime。
3. 文档提示 Agent：长任务应用 unbuffered 或显式 `flush`。

items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## 背景 / 输入

NatureBench 复现会话在 run 前已通过 API 将 `approvalMode` 设为 `always_allow`：

```http
PATCH /api/sessions/{sessionId}
{"approvalMode":"always_allow"}
```

随后 Agent 大量调用工具（读文件、装依赖、跑 python、写报告等）。日志：`jiuwenswarm.log`。

## 问题是什么

即便会话级 `always_allow`，运行中仍出现大量 **`allow_once` 且 `persisted=False`** 风格的授权记录（约百余次量级），审批噪声大、不粘滞。长复现任务的可观测性被权限流水淹没；也与用户对「Always allow = 本会话不再追问」的心智模型不符。

（权限文案/网络同意相关体验另见 #392、#393。）

## 我们怎么规避的

- 仍设 `always_allow`，减少 UI 卡死概率。
- 监控与成功判据改看 workspace 文件与 run 状态，不依赖权限流水是否「干净」。

## 期望应该是什么样

1. `always_allow` 应对该 session（或同 permission epoch）的同类工具调用真正粘滞，而不是每次 `allow_once` + `persisted=False`。
2. 日志/UI 在 always_allow 下折叠或汇总授权，避免百级噪音。
3. 文档写清：哪些动作仍会突破 always_allow（若有硬例外），并与设置文案一致。

## 相关

- #392 Permission card: "Allow same type" is unclear
- #393 Resume after a sandbox network block needs three consecutive approvals
items.title: [Usability] session always_allow still floods allow_once / non-persisted authorizations

items.author: HongyeZhou
items.body:
## Problem
On #381 head `fb2fe785` (Fixes #324), in Ask mode with a domain-allowlist policy, resuming a blocked retrieval takes three cards in a row:
1. **Run a shell script** (approve the original `run_shell`)
2. **Sandbox network** for the observed denied host ("Continue the sandbox retrieval blocked by this execution")
3. **Run a shell script** again, for the NEW `run_shell` that carries `network_authorization_id`

Every step is correct by itself, but together they are heavy for a single user intent ("let this retrieval reach host X").

## Expected
One network decision is enough to resume. The re-run that consumes the one-use network token should not ask again for shell approval the user just gave, as long as it is the same kind of execution.

## Proposal / security considerations
- Reuse the prior shell approval only for the token re-run: same Session/Agent/run, same Runner, and the token is consumed exactly once.
- Do not carry the approval over if the command changes materially. At minimum, show the new command in the network card or require re-approval when it differs from the blocked execution. Otherwise a token re-run becomes a way to run unreviewed code with network access.
- Never inherit Always Allow / direct-execution consent; keep child Agents and later runs excluded, as #381 already does.
- Alternative: merge steps 2 and 3 into a single card ("Allow network to X and re-run this command").

## Context
Refs #381, #324. Observed in a local box run (API + bubblewrap runner + egress gateway, scripted model).

## Verification cases
1. **Baseline repro (current behaviour)**
   - Preconditions: Ask approval mode; sandbox network `domain-allowlist` with `allowedDomains: ["pypi.org"]`; the model calls `run_shell` with `curl -sS -m 8 -o /dev/null -w 'HTTP %{http_code}\n' https://example.com/`.
   - Steps: Allow once on the shell card → allow once on the `example.com:443` network card → the model issues a NEW `run_shell` with the returned `network_authorization_id`.
   - Expected (today): A third "Run a shell script" card appears. After it is approved, the first execution has failed (`CONNECT tunnel failed`, HTTP 000) and the second has completed with HTTP 200 (2 executions in total).
2. **Same command, token re-run: single network decision**
   - Preconditions/Steps: As in 1.
   - Expected (after fix): Exactly 2 cards in total (shell, network). The token re-run with the identical command starts without another shell card and ends with HTTP 200.
3. **Different command must re-ask (security)**
   - Preconditions: As in 1, but the token re-run uses a different command (e.g. appends `; echo changed > marker.txt`).
   - Expected: A shell card is shown again, or the network card displays the new command before approval. It never runs silently.
4. **Token is one-use**
   - Steps: After case 2, the model calls `run_shell` a third time with the same `network_authorization_id`.
   - Expected: The call is rejected ("Unknown, consumed or foreign sandbox network authorization"), and no execution is started.
5. **No carry-over across scope**
   - Steps: Use the token or reused approval from (a) a child Agent, (b) a later run in the same Session, (c) another Runner.
   - Expected: Each is rejected or re-prompts, and no shell approval is reused.
6. **Deny path**
   - Steps: As in 1, but Deny the network card.
   - Expected: No re-run and no third card. The assistant reports the retrieval as blocked/incomplete, and the sandbox network settings are unchanged.
items.title: [Usability] Resume after a sandbox network block needs three consecutive approvals

items.author: HugoXK
items.body:
Follow-up to #245, criterion 3. PR #617 delivers the measurement harness and the per-request wire diagnostics, but the real relay-vs-direct measurement is **not** delivered: the team's bot host has no relay or model endpoint credentials.

## What is missing

Criterion 3 of #245 asks for a comparison of a relay endpoint against a direct endpoint with the same model alias, the same request body bytes, the same workload and the same concurrency, with wire latency reported separately from agent duration and token counts. The harness exists (`scripts/model-endpoint-compare.mjs`, delivered in #617 and covered by `scripts/model-endpoint-compare.test.mjs` against local stub endpoints). What does not exist is a run against real endpoints, so #245 stays open as partially delivered.

## Who can run it

Someone on an owner-hosted machine that has both endpoint URLs and their credentials. The team's bot host cannot: it has no model credentials, and this is not a code problem.

## Command (fill the placeholders)

```bash
node scripts/model-endpoint-compare.mjs \
  --model <model-alias> \
  --prompt-file <one-prompt.txt> \
  --a-name relay  --a-base-url <relay-base-url>  --a-token-env A_TOKEN \
  --b-name direct --b-base-url <direct-base-url> --b-token-env B_TOKEN \
  --requests 20 --concurrency 2 --timeout-ms 300000 \
  --out compare.json
```

`--body-file <identical-body.json>` may be used instead of `--prompt-file` when the exact request body must be reused. The script refuses two different model aliases and refuses a workload where the two bodies would differ, so a latency delta cannot come from a body change.

## What to do with the result

Paste the comparison table the script prints (p50/p90/p95 per endpoint, failures, tokens) and attach or link `compare.json` in #245. That closes criterion 3.

## Notes

- Endpoint tokens are read from the environment variables named by `--a-token-env` / `--b-token-env`; they are never written into the report.
- No repository change is expected from this issue: it is a measurement task, not a code task.

Related: #245, #617.
items.title: [Follow-up] Measure relay vs direct model latency on an owner-hosted endpoint (#245 criterion 3)

items.author: hsliuustc0106
items.body:
## Goal

Make ScienceDiscovery a useful, approachable research product. A researcher should be able to understand what it can help with, get started with clear guidance, complete a task, and return to their work confidently.

The first experience we should deliver is simple:

**Open the app → connect a model → upload a CSV and ask a question → receive a useful chart → refine and save the result.**

The application should handle routine setup and organization, ask only for decisions that matter, and explain the next step in plain language. Technical details should be available when needed.

## Why this matters

During a trial of release 0.2.0, a new user encountered welcome cards that did not navigate, confusing model setup, unexplained `Unauthorized` messages, and an interface that opened even though analysis could not run on that computer. These problems prevented the user from experiencing the product's value.

This evidence comes from one installation. Check fixes in the current release and development branch before opening duplicate work. Related public feedback includes [difficulty finding the download](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/1).

## Improvements

### 1. Make the starting point obvious

- Explain the product with one concrete example and show its finished result.
- Provide prominent **Get started**, **Try an example**, and **Watch the walkthrough** actions.
- Make every suggested action work. Clearly explain unavailable actions and how to enable them.
- Offer a visible English/中文 switch and consistent wording throughout the experience.

### 2. Guide the user through setup

- Provide one recommended download and setup path for each supported computer type.
- Ask for the minimum information needed to connect a model, with helpful defaults and a clear connection test. Explain any required API key, where to obtain it, and that provider usage may incur charges.
- Handle the app's internal connection automatically where possible. If a user must reconnect, take them directly to a guided recovery step.
- Check that analysis can actually run before showing the app as ready. Explain compatibility problems early and provide a concrete next action.
- Keep advanced configuration accessible outside the ordinary setup flow.

### 3. Make everyday work feel straightforward

- Let users start with a question or a file. Create the initial project/session automatically for the guided example.
- Show understandable progress based on what is happening, such as reading data or preparing a chart. Make waiting, required input, completion, and failure easy to distinguish.
- Provide visible stop/retry actions where appropriate. Preserve the user's question and files when something fails.
- Explain errors in plain language with a recovery action; place diagnostic details behind an expandable option.
- Present the result clearly, with an explanation, supporting evidence, and access to the producing code. Make follow-up requests, saving/exporting, and returning later easy to discover.

### 4. Provide two videos that help people understand the product

**Video 1 — From opening the app to a first result (5–7 minutes).** Show a real released version: download/open, connect a model, upload the supplied CSV, ask a question, inspect the chart, request a change, and reopen the saved work. Provide the sample file, prompt, transcript, and English/Chinese captions. Show required preparation and label accelerated waits.

**Video 2 — The same task with and without ScienceDiscovery (6–8 minutes).** Use IMO 2026 Day 2 Problem 5 to compare the same model in direct conversation and in ScienceDiscovery. Focus on the viewer's experience: what they ask, how much guidance they provide, how understandable and complete the answer is, and how easily they can inspect or continue the work. Also report actual time and cost.

Keep the problem, model, and budgets comparable; review the mathematical proofs and report the observed outcome, including ties or failures. The problem's answer is the family `f(x) = x + c`, with `c >= 0`; describe it as the complete solution family. See the [original problem](https://www.imo-official.org/assets/documents/problems/2026/2026_eng.pdf) and [published reference proof](https://github.com/AxiomMath/IMO2026/blob/main/IMO2026/Q5/solution.lean).

Both videos must reflect working released behavior. Their purpose is to explain the experience and demonstrate useful outcomes. Test the app's guidance with new users, including people who have not watched the videos, and fix the points where they get stuck.

### 5. Make feedback and contribution welcoming

- Provide an obvious way to ask for help or report a problem without requiring users to understand the architecture.
- Explain where contributions are reviewed and how GitHub visitors reach that destination. The [current contribution guide](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/blob/907382ce42e1ebfe77e24281905dec0607aaf003/CONTRIBUTING.md) routes code contributions to GitCode.
- Offer a short first-contribution guide and a few bounded tasks with named reviewers. Useful examples include improving a confusing screen, contributing an analysis example, or fixing a connector.
- Document checks newcomers can run without paid model access or special hardware, and how maintainers help with the remaining validation.

## How we know this is better

- [ ] A new user can explain what ScienceDiscovery does and identify how to start.
- [ ] On a supported computer, the user can complete the sample analysis, refine the result, and reopen the saved work without live maintainer assistance.
- [ ] Setup problems are explained before the user starts dependent work; failures preserve their inputs and offer a clear next step.
- [ ] The main journey works in English and Chinese, and the displayed controls and instructions match the released app.
- [ ] Both videos are linked from the project entry page, use actual runs, and include the materials needed to follow or inspect them.
- [ ] A new contributor can find a suitable task, run the relevant checks, submit a change, and understand the review process.

Observe ten unfamiliar users and use eight completing the sample journey without intervention as an initial target. Also record where users get stuck, whether they return the following week, and whether contributors return for another contribution. These are proposed targets, not current results.

## Delivery

Prioritize the first-use journey and recovery from the problems already observed. Validate the downloadable release, record the videos, and improve the experience with a small pilot group before broader promotion. Give each follow-up a named owner.
items.title: [Rfc] Make ScienceDiscovery easy to understand, start, and use

items.author: zy95-12
items.body:
## Background

ScienceDiscovery is strengthening its end-to-end test coverage. We want to collect the complete user journeys that the community believes must remain continuously protected.

This RFC does not prescribe an implementation. It focuses on four questions: **What task is the user trying to complete? What outcomes must be observable? Does the scenario require a real model? Should it run as a pull-request gate or as a scheduled test?**

## How to contribute

Copy the comment template below and add one row for each proposed test scenario. Maintainers will periodically consolidate actionable feedback into the main table.

Guidelines:

- **Test scenario**: describe a complete flow from the user's goal, rather than an internal function or an isolated component.
- **Observations**: list user-visible outcomes and critical states, such as the final answer, tool calls, permissions, artifacts, citations, and recovery after a refresh.
- **Test method**: use `Mock LLM`, `Real LLM`, or `Both`, and explain why a real model is necessary when applicable.
- **Estimated token usage**: use `0 (scripted)` for Mock LLM cases; for Real LLM cases, estimate total input and output tokens for one run.
- **Estimated duration**: give the target duration for one case, excluding first-time dependency installation.
- **Priority**: use `P0` for basic platform availability, `P1` for core scientific capabilities, and `P2` for enhancements or corner cases.
- **Notes**: record environment requirements, external services, credentials, cost, side effects, candidate benchmark sources, or stability risks.

## Initial candidates

The following entries are both examples of the requested format and an initial backlog. The community is welcome to refine their priority, observations, estimates, and execution method.

| Test scenario | Observations | Test method (Mock or Real LLM) | Related feature | Estimated token usage | Estimated duration | Priority | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Basic multi-turn conversation and refresh recovery | The run completes; the second turn uses conversation history; message order, terminal state, and refreshed content remain consistent | Mock LLM | Session, Agent Loop, History, SSE | 0 (scripted) | 2–3 min | P0 | No external network |
| Tool call, permission, and continued reasoning | Permission moves from pending to allowed; the tool executes once; its result returns to the model; the Agent continues and finishes | Mock LLM | Tool, Permission, Runner, Agent Loop | 0 (scripted) | 2–3 min | P0 | Use a safe local tool fixture |
| Plan creation, update, and completion | Plan and step states remain ordered and correct; updates do not block tools; the final state persists and recovers | Mock LLM | Plan, Context, Workspace UI | 0 (scripted) | 2–3 min | P0 | Use a deterministic tool-call sequence |
| Subagent delegation and result return | The child Agent lifecycle is complete; tool ownership is correct; the result returns to the lead Agent; reasoning continues; refresh restores the state | Mock LLM | Subagent, Team, Tool, Context | 0 (scripted) | 3–4 min | P0 | No external provider |
| Generate and deliver an artifact | The file exists; deliverables are distinct from temporary files; preview and download work; provenance is traceable; the final answer references the artifact | Mock LLM | Workspace, Artifact, Provenance, Tool | 0 (scripted) | 3–4 min | P0 | Use a local Python or Shell environment |
| Literature review | The Agent searches multiple sources, retrieves and extracts selected papers, produces traceable citations, handles source failures, and delivers a review artifact | Both | MCP, Literature Sources, Governed Download, PDF Extraction, Citation, Review | 0 mocked; 20k–60k real | 10–30 min | P1 | Real run requires network access and may depend on source availability |
| Evolve a solution | The Agent defines an objective and evaluation, runs iterative candidates, preserves checkpoints and logs, compares results, and delivers the best reproducible solution | Both | Evolve, Runner, Artifact, Provenance, Review | 0 mocked; 15k–50k real | 10–30 min | P1 | Candidate source: Terminal-Bench-Science |
| Data analysis | The Agent inspects an input dataset, selects and executes a valid analysis, validates intermediate results, and delivers reproducible code, figures, and conclusions | Both | Workspace, Python/R, Artifact, Provenance, Review | 0 mocked; 10k–40k real | 10–25 min | P1 | Candidate source: BiomniBench-DA |
| AI model workflow | The Agent prepares valid model inputs, invokes the model workload, exposes execution progress, preserves outputs and environment metadata, and explains the result | Both | Scientific Environment, Runner, NPU, Artifact, Provenance | 0 mocked; 10k–40k real | 15–60 min | P1 | Candidate tools/models: Protenix, ProteinMPNN, and similar workloads; hardware availability may constrain scheduling |
| Simulation tool workflow | The Agent prepares a valid simulation, invokes the selected simulator, reports progress and failures, and delivers reproducible configuration, logs, and results | Both | Scientific Environment, Runner, Tool, Artifact, Provenance | 0 mocked; 10k–40k real | 15–60 min | P1 | Real cases may require licensed software, large dependencies, or specialized hardware |
| Memory graph | Research outputs are written to the graph with correct identities and relations; retrieval returns relevant prior context; graph-backed citations remain traceable after refresh | Both | Memory Graph, Context, Provenance, Citation | 0 mocked; 8k–25k real | 5–20 min | P1 | Mocked case can use the local backend; scheduled case may use Neo4j |
| Agent team collaboration | The lead Agent decomposes work across multiple specialists; child scopes remain isolated; progress is observable; results return to the lead and are synthesized without loss or duplication | Both | Agent Team, Subagent, Context, Permission, Trajectory | 0 mocked; 15k–50k real | 10–30 min | P1 | Include concurrent child execution and one recoverable child failure |
| Idea Tree research | The Agent starts an Idea Tree run, expands and evaluates candidates, supports pause and resume, persists the tree, and delivers the selected result with its reasoning trail | Both | Idea Tree, Evolve, Workspace UI, Artifact, Provenance | 0 mocked; 15k–50k real | 10–30 min | P1 | Validate both tree state and the user-visible explorer |

## Comment template

Copy this table into a comment. Add more rows when proposing multiple scenarios.

| Test scenario | Observations | Test method (Mock or Real LLM) | Related feature | Estimated token usage | Estimated duration | Priority | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Describe the complete user journey | List user-visible outcomes and critical states | Mock LLM / Real LLM / Both | List related capabilities | Estimate | Estimate | P0 / P1 / P2 | Add environment, cost, dependency, or stability notes |

## Suggested areas

- Agent Loop, tools, permissions, planning, and Agent teams;
- MCP, skills, Web Search, and Web Fetch;
- literature retrieval, paper download, PDF extraction, and scientific databases;
- artifacts, provenance, evidence, claims, citations, and review;
- context compression, long-running task continuity, and error recovery;
- local and remote Runners, scientific environments, NPU workloads, and background tasks;
- settings, onboarding, observability, and critical usability journeys;
- scenarios that can reveal issues only with a Real LLM or a real external service.

## Expected outcome

Community feedback will form a prioritized E2E case backlog, divided into:

- fast Mocked E2E cases executed for every pull request;
- comprehensive Mocked and Real LLM E2E cases executed on a schedule;
- real scientific-task acceptance tests executed before a release.

This issue is for collecting and clarifying test requirements. Implementation can be split into follow-up issues and pull requests by scenario.

## Summary and current-release boundary

Multi-agent orchestration is a core JiuwenSwarm capability. ScienceDiscovery should explicitly evaluate whether and how to reuse it, rather than silently treating our existing orchestration as the final architecture.

For this release, retain the currently validated hybrid path: **ScienceDiscovery manages delegation through `task`; JiuwenSwarm executes both the main agent and the child agents.** This RFC does not request an immediate migration or block the current release. The eventual reuse decision must be documented with implementation evidence, validation results, and trade-offs.

## Current implementation

The current debugging deployment explicitly selects the platform `task` route. This is a deployment choice, not a claim that every Swarm-backed deployment uses this route.

```text
Main agent (Swarm loop)
  -> ScienceDiscovery task orchestration
  -> Child agent (independent Swarm loop)
  -> Platform task result
  -> Main agent continues
```

ScienceDiscovery currently prepares the specialist profile, enabled MCP/skills, workspace and handoff; manages permissions, concurrency, turn/time limits and cancellation; and records child progress, results and artifacts for the existing UI. The parent receives the result when the `task` call completes.

Swarm's native route uses `subagent_spawn` and `subagent_wait`, with Swarm owning child orchestration. Its integration with ScienceDiscovery-specific bindings has not been fully validated. This does **not** mean Swarm lacks tools, permissions or lifecycle management; the question is how its mechanisms map to the platform's existing behavior.

## Problem and existing evidence

Using Swarm only as the execution engine leaves an important part of its core capability unreused, while switching delegation tools alone risks losing platform behavior. We need a deliberate ownership boundary instead of two overlapping orchestration systems.

A recent real-LLM literature-research run completed through platform `task`: two Swarm-executed children used professional literature MCP tools, returned results, and the parent produced a registered report. This validates that hybrid route only; it does not establish native `subagent_spawn` MCP inheritance, comparative quality, or benchmark-wide reliability.

## Evaluation scope

Evaluate the native route against the current hybrid baseline on the same pinned versions and comparable model/task/tool settings.

| Area | Questions to resolve |
| --- | --- |
| Delegation and scheduling | Who owns creation, concurrency, waiting, completion, and nested delegation? Can we avoid duplicate schedulers and inconsistent state? |
| Context and capabilities | How do specialist instructions, skills, model selection and enabled MCP tools reach each child's actual LLM input? What is inherited versus explicitly handed off? |
| Workspace and science outputs | How do child workspace isolation, sandbox paths, artifact registration, provenance and parent access map to Swarm? |
| Permissions and lifecycle | How are manual approval, automatic approval, cancellation, turn/time limits and partial failures preserved? |
| Results and UI | How are streaming child progress, tool events, usage, errors and final results represented in the existing UI? Does the parent reliably continue? |
| Maintenance | Which extension points already exist? Which minimal upstream fixes/hooks are missing? What platform code could actually be removed? |

Prefer native Swarm capabilities for generic agent behavior. Keep differentiated science functionality in separate modules; intrusive Swarm changes should be limited to bug fixes or necessary extension hooks, not embedding science business logic.

## Candidate outcomes — not a predetermined selection

1. **Native Swarm orchestration plus science extensions:** reuse spawning/waiting/lifecycle and adapt platform capabilities and UI events.
2. **Staged migration:** retain `task` temporarily while closing named native-integration gaps, then transfer ownership with clear exit criteria.
3. **Retain platform orchestration:** acceptable only with concrete evidence explaining why native reuse is unsuitable, its maintenance costs, and conditions for revisiting the decision.

A tool rename or a single successful demo is insufficient to choose between these options.

## Validation and required conclusion

The decision should be backed by deterministic integration tests and a small set of comparable real research runs, not only code inspection.

- Verify actual child LLM tool lists, model routing, skill/context delivery and workspace access.
- Cover parallel children, successful result collection and parent continuation, one child failing, timeout/cancellation, and both approval modes.
- Verify child artifacts remain accessible and traceable, and UI progress reaches a correct terminal state.
- Compare task completion, result quality, token use, elapsed time and resource consumption under comparable conditions; record limitations and failures.

Before closing this RFC, publish a community-reviewed conclusion containing:

- the selected architecture and the rationale for reusing or not reusing native Swarm orchestration;
- a capability/gap matrix with concrete source or test evidence;
- ownership of scheduling, context/tool binding, permissions, lifecycle and science outputs;
- required changes, migration and rollback boundaries, and code that can be removed;
- remaining limitations and follow-up issues, with an explicit distinction between current-release acceptance and the long-term decision.

Related: #84 (Swarm migration), #107 (E2E scenarios).
items.title: [Rfc] Evaluate native JiuwenSwarm multi-agent orchestration versus the current platform task integration

# 中文版

## 版本定位

ScienceDiscovery **`0.3.0-rc1`** 与 [`0.3.0-beta`](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/releases/tag/0.3.0-beta) 同属 **0.3.0 正式版前的预发布版本**：在既有 JiuwenSwarm 科研工作台能力之上，继续收敛质量与工程化交付，为正式版做候选验证。

上一版本为 `0.3.0-beta`（2026-09-30）。本版本汇总 **2026-10-01 → 2026-10-16**（Asia/Shanghai）已合并进 `main` 的变更。

> 本文是面向社区征求意见的 **Release Note 草案**，不是正式发版公告；正式 GitHub Release / tag 将另发。

## Release Note 草案

### 新功能

- **L1–L5 多级 CI 门禁**：按 PR → merge → daily → release 分层累积质量检查，Nightly/Release 真实 E2E 与 hermetic 检查并行落地（#259，相关 #280、#255、#258）。

### 主要修复

- **沙箱 / Runner 未就绪**：启动与 Runner 就绪解耦；执行仍 fail-closed；Agent 可通过 `check_runner` / `wait_for_runner` 等待，并弹出重试/切换/取消恢复卡片；区分「展示等待」与「授权修复」（#275 / #265，#282）。
- **不可解析 tool call**：长科研 run 中改为扣留并恢复，不再误报为模型配置错误并整段结束主/子 Agent（#247 / #236）。
- **自定义模型设置**：任一设置接口失败时保留 provider 预设，避免 Custom provider 空表单卡死（#288 / #281）。
- **交付签收**：接受带可选章节号的 Methods/Results/References，避免临近预算误触发重写（#294 / #292）。
- **产物提交**：CAS ref commit 复用已校验对象元数据，降低长轨迹提交开销（#250；#230 仍开）。
- **真实 E2E 稳定化**：J5 等待托管 Python（#287 / #286）；主 Agent run 链完成后再做终局断言（#253）；中断时保留已完成旅程证据（#266 / #263）；Nightly flaky 断言（#207、#279）；L3 改为真实用户旅程（#272）。
- **CI 配套**：job 重跑覆盖同名 artifact（#302 / #301）；分数与诊断产物分离（#240）；Mock E2E 四 worker、UT 并行等（#273、#277、#268、#242）；Biomni DA-13-3 / DA-14-1 恢复进 daily/release，Nightly 结构化挂载 `science-research-team`（#270、#306）。

### 行为变更

- 启动不再强依赖本地沙箱可用；未就绪时执行被拒绝，需经恢复流程后再下发（#275）。
- Nightly Biomni 挂载 `science-research-team` 后，分数不可与 beta 裸题基线直接对比（#306）。

<details>
<summary>已合并 PR（28）</summary>

#207 #240 #242 #243 #244 #247 #250 #253 #255 #256 #258 #259 #266 #268 #270 #272 #273 #275 #277 #279 #280 #282 #287 #288 #294 #300 #302 #306

</details>

## 社区反馈

欢迎在本 Issue 讨论：

- 草案表述是否清楚、是否遗漏重要合入
- RC1 作为正式版前候选，你最关心的验证场景
- 文案、分类或中英对照的改进建议

请尽量附上复现步骤、日志或相关 PR/Issue 链接。

---

# English version

## Release positioning

ScienceDiscovery **`0.3.0-rc1`**, like [`0.3.0-beta`](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/releases/tag/0.3.0-beta), is a **pre-release ahead of the formal 0.3.0**. It builds on the existing JiuwenSwarm scientific workbench and continues to tighten quality and delivery engineering as a release candidate.

The previous version is `0.3.0-beta` (2026-09-30). This draft covers changes merged into `main` from **2026-10-01 through 2026-10-16** (Asia/Shanghai).

> This is a **community draft** for feedback, not a formal release announcement. The GitHub Release / tag will be published separately.

## Draft release notes

### New features

- **L1–L5 multi-level CI gates**: layered quality checks across PR → merge → daily → release, with Nightly/Release real E2E alongside hermetic checks (#259; related #280, #255, #258).

### Major fixes

- **Sandbox / Runner not ready**: decouple workbench startup from Runner readiness; execution remains fail-closed; the Agent can wait via `check_runner` / `wait_for_runner` and present retry / switch / cancel recovery cards; distinguish “show waiting UI” from “authorize repair” (#275 / #265, #282).
- **Unparseable tool calls**: hold and recover during long research runs instead of misreporting a model-configuration error and killing the main or sub-Agent (#247 / #236).
- **Custom model settings**: keep provider presets when any settings request fails, avoiding a stuck empty Custom provider form (#288 / #281).
- **Deliverable acceptance**: accept Methods/Results/References headings with optional section numbers so near-budget rewrites are not triggered incorrectly (#294 / #292).
- **Artifact commits**: reuse validated object metadata on the CAS ref-commit path to cut long-trajectory commit cost (#250; #230 remains open).
- **Real E2E stabilization**: wait for managed Python on J5 (#287 / #286); assert only after the main Agent run chain completes (#253); retain completed-journey evidence on interrupt (#266 / #263); Nightly flaky assertions (#207, #279); L3 as real user journeys (#272).
- **CI follow-ups**: overwrite same-named artifacts on job re-run (#302 / #301); separate score and diagnostic artifacts (#240); Mock E2E four workers and UT parallelism (#273, #277, #268, #242); restore Biomni DA-13-3 / DA-14-1 to daily/release and structurally attach `science-research-team` on Nightly (#270, #306).

### Behavior changes

- Startup no longer requires a ready local sandbox; execution is rejected until recovery completes (#275).
- After Nightly Biomni attaches `science-research-team`, scores are not directly comparable to the beta bare-prompt baseline (#306).

</details>

## Community feedback

Please comment on this issue with:

- Whether the draft is clear or missing important merges
- Scenarios you care most about validating for RC1
- Wording, categorization, or bilingual improvements

Include repro steps, logs, or related PR/issue links when possible.

## Summary

On 2026-10-26 every GitHub issue in `openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery` was classified against the nine requirement rows in #249. Pull requests were excluded. The three counts agreed: `gh issue list --state all`, REST pagination of 100 items per page, and the issue search counter. The total is **232** issues, **116 open** and **116 closed**.

Whether an issue is developed was judged from `origin/main` at `65eddde1`, not from the open or closed flag. An open issue can already be on `main`. A closed issue can still be undeveloped when it was closed as a duplicate or as not planned, or when the change never reached `main`.

This issue records that snapshot. It does not close, retitle, or implement any of the issues below.

## Counts

| | |
| --- | --- |
| bug / feature / other | 73 / 151 / 8 |
| bug severity P0 / P1 / P2 / P3 | 1 / 24 / 44 / 4 |
| mapped to a #249 row / unmapped | 139 / 93 |
| developed / partial / not developed / not applicable | 103 / 39 / 82 / 8 |
| marked complex | 122 |

Severity is the impact of the defect itself. It is not lowered because a later commit fixed it. "Not applicable" is used only for the eight items in **other**, which have no defect or feature to build. "Complex" means the work crosses modules, depends on an external system, or packs several independent pieces into one issue.

## Rules

1. An issue maps to one of the nine names in the #249 table, or to **unmapped**.
2. Issues already closed before the 2026-10-10 v0.3.0 kickoff stay unmapped, even when the topic matches a row. An issue closed on 2026-10-10 counts as inside the cycle. This rule sets aside 20 topic matches: CI engineering refactor 4, componentized architecture 10, documentation and website 5, routine bug fixes 1. Those four counts are part of the snapshot. The 20 issue numbers are not listed separately.
3. A feature maps by topic and never lands in Routine bug fixes.
4. A bug in behavior that a requirement row delivers maps to that row. Other bugs inside the release cycle map to Routine bug fixes.
5. A defect in the test or CI harness (a wrong gate, lost end-to-end evidence, broken test discovery) maps to CI engineering refactor. A product defect that CI happened to catch still maps to Routine bug fixes.
6. **Other** is a calendar, a call for release-note feedback, a discussion, or a usage question. #249 itself is other and unmapped: it is the calendar that holds the table.
7. Developed means the requested behavior is on `origin/main` at `65eddde1`. Evidence is a merge that is an ancestor of that commit, or a path on that commit. Early pull requests, roughly #3 through #111, were rewritten out of that ancestry and were checked by subject or by path. A number in an older write-up that is actually a GitCode id was not treated as a GitHub pull request.
8. Closed as duplicate or not planned stays **not developed**, even when the same behavior later arrived through another issue.
   - #405 was closed as a duplicate of #406. The behavior landed with #406 in pull request #407. #405 stays not developed.
   - #327 was closed as not planned and superseded by #330. The behavior landed with #330 in pull request #356. #327 stays not developed.

## Requirement rows

Bug / feature / other, then developed / partial / not developed / not applicable.

| #249 requirement | Hit | bug / feature / other | developed / partial / not developed / n/a | Issues |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CI engineering refactor (#248) | 22 | 14 / 8 / 0 | 12 / 7 / 3 / 0 | #126, #175, #232, #233, #234, #239, #245, #248, #251, #252, #260, #263, #283, #286, #292, #301, #346, #350, #423, #444, #514, #519 |
| Installation experience / desktop client delivery (#400) | 28 | 3 / 25 / 0 | 4 / 6 / 18 / 0 | #22, #29, #31, #32, #34, #37, #38, #264, #265, #305, #313, #400, #476, #477, #479, #481, #482, #483, #485, #487, #489, #491, #493, #495, #496, #505, #506, #507 |
| Componentized ScienceDiscovery architecture and WorkSwarm boundary | 16 | 2 / 14 / 0 | 0 / 7 / 9 / 0 | #84, #85, #93, #94, #96, #98, #99, #100, #101, #102, #104, #105, #106, #141, #257, #410 |
| Documentation and official website content (#399) | 11 | 1 / 10 / 0 | 6 / 3 / 2 / 0 | #25, #26, #27, #30, #46, #55, #117, #118, #312, #332, #399 |
| System configuration and in-conversation settings / resume (#278) | 6 | 1 / 5 / 0 | 2 / 0 / 4 / 0 | #39, #44, #66, #278, #452, #462 |
| Routine bug fixes | 49 | 49 / 0 / 0 | 36 / 2 / 11 / 0 | #35, #36, #40, #45, #49, #67, #68, #208, #210, #235, #236, #237, #238, #246, #281, #284, #290, #291, #296, #298, #299, #307, #314, #325, #326, #334, #335, #337, #365, #366, #367, #368, #369, #370, #371, #413, #414, #429, #430, #435, #445, #446, #461, #469, #471, #484, #557, #558, #559 |
| NPU task state recovery after disconnections or errors (#398) | 3 | 2 / 1 / 0 | 1 / 1 / 1 / 0 | #185, #398, #541 |
| Recovery of failed long-running tasks (#401) | 2 | 0 / 2 / 0 | 0 / 1 / 1 / 0 | #170, #401 |
| Build an initial automated development pipeline | 2 | 0 / 2 / 0 | 0 / 0 / 2 / 0 | #376, #422 |
| Unmapped | 93 | 1 / 84 / 8 | 42 / 12 / 31 / 8 | not enumerated here |

## Severity that is already on main

The only P0 is #371, MCP TypeScript SDK 1.30.0 below the OAuth credential-binding fix. It is closed and developed: pull request #374 is an ancestor of `65eddde1`, and `services/api` resolves `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` to 1.31.0. It stays P0 because the rating records the impact of persisting a refresh token where that advisory applied, not the current open state.

#369 (undici below 8.10.2; `main` has 8.12.2) and #370 (katex below 0.18.2; `main` has 0.18.10, including the copy brought in by rehype-katex) are P1, and both are also developed in #374. They are P1 rather than P0 because the classification did not find evidence that those advisories were reachable in this product's use.

## Open bugs not fully on that main commit

These GitHub issues were still open on 2026-10-26, and the requested behavior was not fully present on `65eddde1`.

**P1**

- #257 Isolate embedded JiuwenSwarm data from a standalone install on the same machine. Not developed.
- #264 Proxy-aware installation: declare SOCKS support and unify preflight and recovery. Partial.
- #410 Cannot release a lock on a filesystem read/write lock database that this task does not hold. Not developed.
- #445 A manual MCP download waits for approval, and the approval action is not discoverable. Not developed.
- #452 After a failed first model connection, Save & connect still fails until the process restarts. Not developed. Also in the uncertain list below.
- #461 A deep data directory breaks the egress socket path, so every `run_shell` fails while the Runner still looks healthy. Not developed.

**P2**

- #49 Idea Tree budget and assessor fields are stored, then overwritten by the intensity preset. Not developed.
- #208 Parallel research agents keep requesting arXiv after repeated 406 and 429 responses. Not developed.
- #232 Nightly real end-to-end treats one transient model-gateway 500 or 503 as a product failure. Not developed.
- #235 A failed model round is shown only as "interaction round execution failed". Not developed.
- #239 A team real end-to-end budget failure reports a run that is still running as a delivery failure. Partial.
- #251 The run-cancel queue test counts JiuwenSwarm's own skill-index build as a second run. Partial.
- #335 Agent tool calls fail and then recover mid-run. Partial.
- #413 Reviewer Specialist still defaults off, so automatic review is unavailable. Partial.
- #435 Automatic review accepts an incomplete reproduce report and goes stale after the artifact changes. Not developed.
- #471 A project cannot be deleted. Not developed. Also in the uncertain list below.
- #519 Nightly session-title assertion, failed-shard accounting, and two unit-test timeouts. Partial.
- #541 An unconfirmed shell observation is stored as a failed execution run. Not developed.
- #557 The assessment-screening skill references `rubric-overall.md`, which does not exist. Not developed.

**P3**

- #429 Dataset table cells are right-aligned under left-aligned headers. Not developed.
- #505 One bad server-sent event frame ends the desktop run stream. Not developed.
- #558 The report-writer skill has an unmatched code fence, and `skills/` is outside the markdownlint globs. Not developed.
- #559 Skill-package validation accepts an empty description that the docs forbid. Not developed.

#423 was still open, rated P2, and already developed on `65eddde1` (`pnpm ci:ut` no longer stops before discovery because the JiuwenSwarm patch target is missing). #210 was still open, rated P1, and already developed (the local memory-graph folded-subgraph query is bounded).

## Could not judge developed or not

- #170 Literature-research handoffs. The issue states a direction and does not give acceptance criteria, so a skill-text instruction to resume is not enough to call it done. Counted as partial under recovery of failed long-running tasks.
- #398 NPU task recovery. Pull request #542 reconciles remote execution in general. Whether that is a partial landing of the NPU requirement needs the owner. Counted as partial.
- #452 The report does not include the version, the second connection error, or a root cause, so later model-setting changes on `main` cannot be shown to fix it. Counted as not developed.
- #471 Deleting a project fails, without the failing request or a server stack. It is not possible to tell a fix on `main` from an old build or a WSL2-only failure. Counted as not developed.

## Other

These eight have no deliverable defect or feature. Development status is not applicable, and all eight are unmapped.

- #1 How to obtain the binary package. Answered as a usage question.
- #48 Feedback comparing this project with other 2026 science workbenches.
- #107 Call for end-to-end scenarios the community wants protected. The issue itself specifies no implementation.
- #213 JiuwenSwarm beta release notes and feedback. Closed as superseded by #343.
- #229 Website launch notes and feedback.
- #249 October 2026 release calendar.
- #274 "Add API failed". Closed without a reproducing defect. The reporter then saved the provider after filling the access token.
- #343 v0.3.0-rc1 release notes and feedback.

items.author: Birfy
items.body:
## Summary

Remote execution today reaches exactly two kinds of target: a machine you can SSH into, and a Slurm cluster. There is no way to run a job on cloud compute — no serverless GPU, no Kubernetes, no cloud VM. A researcher without an HPC allocation or a GPU workstation has no path to accelerated compute at all.

## Current state

The remote-compute model is already well factored, which is why this is an extension rather than a rewrite:

- `RemoteHostConnectionKind = "direct" | "ssh"` — the product either deploys a Runner SEA over SSH (verified host key, SHA-256 checked upload, HTTP tunneled through SSH) or connects to a runner the user started.
- `RemoteJobCard` carries `command`, `inputPaths`, `outputs`, `resources`, `targetAlias`, and `mode: "slurm" | "ssh"`.
- Jobs pass through an approval step (`approvedAt`) before anything runs.
- The host probe records CPU, memory, architecture, scratch paths, and whether Slurm is present — and accepts Linux only.
- Ascend NPU has a dedicated host broker.

So the concepts a cloud backend needs — a job card, declared inputs and outputs, a resource request, an approval gate, a target registry — all exist. What is missing is a third `mode`.

## Why it matters

The Slurm and SSH paths assume the user already has institutional compute. Everyone else — an individual researcher, a small lab, anyone whose cluster queue is full — is limited to the local sandbox. Meanwhile a comparable open-source workbench offers user-owned serverless GPU runs bound to an approved image digest, which is exactly the "I need a GPU for twenty minutes" case we cannot serve.

## Proposal

### 1. A `cloud` job mode behind the existing card + approval model

Define a small provider interface — submit(image digest, command, inputs, resources) → poll status → fetch outputs → report cost — and let backends implement it. The job card, the approval UI, and the output staging stay as they are.

### 2. First backend: Kubernetes Job

Recommended as the first implementation, ahead of any specific vendor:

- works against on-prem clusters, every major cloud, and local clusters for testing;
- no vendor lock-in in a project whose selling point is being model- and vendor-agnostic;
- resource requests, GPU scheduling, and namespaces map cleanly onto `RemoteJobResources`;
- credentials are the user's own kubeconfig, not a service we broker.

A serverless GPU provider can follow once the interface has one real implementation behind it.

### 3. Keep the security contract explicit

Cloud execution is a bigger step than SSH to a known host, because **data leaves the workstation**. So:

- the approval card must show exactly which files are uploaded, where, and to whose account;
- image references must be content-addressed digests, not mutable tags;
- credentials stay user-owned; the product must never proxy compute through an account we control;
- an air-gapped deployment must be able to disable cloud targets entirely;
- show an estimated cost before approval — the governance and quota machinery already exists to hang this on.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A third job mode exists alongside `ssh` and `slurm`, reusing the current job-card and approval flow.
- [ ] At least one backend runs a GPU job end to end: inputs uploaded, job executed, outputs retrieved into the workspace.
- [ ] The approval card states what data leaves the machine and where it goes.
- [ ] Image references are digests.
- [ ] Cloud targets can be disabled by policy for restricted deployments.
- [ ] Failure modes — quota exceeded, image pull failure, job evicted — surface as actionable errors, not a stalled job.

## Open questions

- Kubernetes first, or a serverless GPU provider first for time-to-value?
- Should the cloud backend reuse the Runner SEA inside the container, or invoke the sandboxed executor directly?
- How should cost estimation work when pricing is provider-specific — a per-target rate the user configures?
- Does the Ascend NPU broker share this interface, or stay a separate path?

items.body:
## Summary

There is no update mechanism of any kind: `autoUpdate` / `checkForUpdate` appear nowhere in the codebase. A user who installed a binary months ago has no way to learn that a newer release exists, short of visiting the repository. Comparable workbenches ship auto-updating desktop builds; we do not even notify.

## Current state

- **Version is visible, staleness is not.** `ScienceDiscovery version` prints the release version plus bundled Node/CPython/micromamba versions. Nothing ever compares that against what has since been published.
- **Releases already carry the right metadata.** `scripts/package-binary-release.sh` emits `VERSION` and `SHA256SUMS` next to the artifacts, and the binary-release flow already verifies downloads by pinned SHA-256 (that is how Node, CPython, micromamba, and the uv wheel are fetched). The building blocks for a verifiable update check exist.
- **Side-by-side versions already work.** The payload cache is digest-keyed (`~/.cache/science-discovery/payload/<payload-id>`) and "an upgrade does not overwrite an older extraction", so an older release stays runnable — rollback is feasible today.
- **Remote runners can silently drift.** The Runner SEA is versioned by the build's Git commit prefix, and a mismatch between the local control plane and an already-deployed remote runner only produces a warning; it does not block or redeploy. So a long-lived SSH target can keep running a months-old runner.
- **No documented upgrade contract.** There is no guide covering data-directory compatibility across releases, what a new binary rebuilds on first `serve`, or how to roll back (also noted in [#25](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/25)).

## Proposal

### 1. Update check (the part that matters most)

An opt-in check against a published release manifest — the existing `VERSION` + `SHA256SUMS` pair is already close to one.

- **Off by default in air-gapped installs**, and settable in system configuration. No telemetry beyond fetching the manifest; do not send an install identifier.
- Route the request through the configured network proxy, since proxy settings already exist.
- Surface the result quietly: a dismissible banner in the UI, a line in `ScienceDiscovery version`, and an explicit `--check-updates` for scripts.
- Fail silent on a network error. An offline workstation must never see an error toast because an update check could not reach the internet.

### 2. Self-update (optional second step)

`ScienceDiscovery update` that downloads the new artifact, verifies it against `SHA256SUMS` (ideally a signature too), swaps it atomically, and keeps the previous binary so a rollback is one command. The digest-keyed payload cache means the old version's extracted runtime is still there.

For Docker and source mode, print the right command instead of attempting anything — `docker compose pull` / `git pull && ./scripts/start-stack.sh` — rather than pretending a binary self-update applies.

### 3. Upgrade contract

Document, and enforce in code:

- what the data directory guarantees across versions, and what the first `serve` after an upgrade rebuilds;
- refusing to open a data directory written by a newer release, rather than half-migrating it;
- redeploying the matching Runner SEA to remote hosts when the control plane updates, instead of only warning about the mismatch.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A user on an outdated release is told so, in the UI and on the CLI.
- [ ] The check is opt-in/opt-out, proxy-aware, and silent on failure.
- [ ] No update path installs an artifact whose SHA-256 was not verified.
- [ ] Rollback to the previous version is documented and works.
- [ ] Docker and source-mode users get correct upgrade instructions rather than a binary self-update.
- [ ] Remote runner drift is resolved automatically or reported as an actionable error.

## Open questions

- Where would the release manifest live, given the canonical repository is on GitCode and GitHub is a mirror? It needs one stable URL.
- Should releases be signed, or is SHA-256 against a manifest over HTTPS sufficient for this threat model?
- Default for the update check on a fresh install: on or off?
items.title: [Feature] Notify users of new releases, and support self-update

items.body:
## Summary

ScienceDiscovery can already evolve the things a user brings it — a program, a prompt, a protocol. It cannot evolve **itself**. I would like RSI support: given a dataset of tasks, search over the agent's own harness — system prompt fragments, specialist instructions, skill methodology, tool and skill selection — score each variant by running it against that dataset, and surface the winner for a human to adopt.

The search machinery for this already exists in `services/evolve`. What is missing is the candidate being the harness, the evaluation being an agent run, and a reviewed promotion step.

## What is already there

This is deliberately an extension, not a new engine.

- **The search sidecar**, `services/evolve`, runs on `agentdescent>=0.4.6` — `evolve()` / `async_evolve()`, `FlatPuct`, the ledger, the verifier and the policies — behind two engines: flat-PUCT tree search (`puct_engine.py`) and MAP-Elites islands with ring migration (`openevolve_engine.py`).
- **Non-program candidates are first class.** `text_candidate.py` exists precisely because "a prompt or an abstract has no docstring", and `judge_domain.py` states its purpose plainly: it "is what makes `/evolve` work on things that are not programs over tables: a prompt, an abstract, a protocol, a plan". Evolving prompt text is not a new capability — it is the existing one pointed at a different file.
- **Four scoring seams**, already cut: `scorecard_domain` (a metric over a dataset), `test_gate_domain` (a suite's pass rate), `script_domain` (a scorer the drafting model writes), `judge_domain` (a rubric read by a model).
- **Anti-reward-hacking is already solved once.** `test_gate_domain` freezes in two layers — a proposal filter over `frozen` globs in the prompt, and enforcement below it — with the upstream note this issue should quote rather than restate: *"without it the shortest path to a high score is to weaken the thing measuring it."* That is the single most important property RSI needs, and the pattern is in the tree.
- **Held-out splitting exists.** `create_evolve_run` already accepts `caseSplit` with `gateGroups`, `rolloutGroups` and `testGroups`, which is the shape needed to keep a harness from overfitting the tasks it was tuned on.
- **Trajectories are recorded.** `packages/trajectory` captures per-session entries with the context blocks that were actually sent, which is the raw material for judging whether a harness change helped.
- **Parts of the harness are already frozen.** Built-in specialists reject edits to `instructions` / `description` / `name` / `connectorIds` / `enabledSkillIds`; only `enabled` is user-mutable. RSI has to open that door deliberately rather than by accident.

## What is missing

1. **The candidate is never the harness.** Today a candidate is one text-shaped artifact the user owns. The agent's own scaffolding lives elsewhere and is not reachable by a search: prompt assembly (`packages/context/src/prompt-renderer.ts`, `assembler.ts`), specialist instructions (`packages/specialist/src/builtins.ts`), skill methodology (`skills/*/SKILL.md`), and the skill/connector selection for a run.

2. **There is no task-dataset scoring mode.** `scorecard_domain` scores a *program* over a table. RSI needs to score a *harness* over a set of tasks, where each evaluation is a full agent run with its own tool calls, sandboxed execution and artifacts. That is a different cost class and needs its own domain.

3. **There is no promotion path.** An improved harness must be diffable, reviewable, versioned and revertible. Nothing should ever be self-applied.

## Proposal

### 1. A harness candidate

A bundle rather than a single blob: prompt fragments, one or more specialist instruction sets, selected skills, and the run settings that go with them. The mutation prompt sees the bundle and rewrites part of it; the ledger records which part changed, so a win is attributable to something specific.

### 2. A `task_dataset` domain

A dataset entry is a task plus whatever the existing four modes need to score its outcome — a metric, a test suite, a scoring script, or a rubric. Evaluating one candidate means running the agent over the split and aggregating. Reuse `caseSplit` so the reported number comes from tasks the search did not tune against.

The honest problem here is cost: one candidate equals N agent runs, each with model calls and sandboxed execution. The design needs a budget per generation and an early-abandon policy, not just a score.

### 3. Freeze the things a self-improving search must not touch

Same two-layer shape `test_gate_domain` already uses, with a wider frozen set:

- the task dataset and its expected outcomes;
- the scorer, whichever mode it is;
- the permission, sandbox and approval layers — a harness that scores better by asking for fewer confirmations is not better;
- the evolve sidecar's own code and the freeze list itself.

A candidate that edits any of these is rejected at the proposal filter, not merely penalized.

### 4. Promotion is a human step

The winner lands as a reviewable proposal: a diff against the current harness, the score with its held-out number, and the trajectory evidence behind it. Adoption is explicit, versioned and revertible. The skill review flow and the built-in specialists' read-only rules already establish that shape; RSI should reuse it rather than invent a second one.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A search can take the agent's harness as its candidate, not only a user artifact.
- [ ] A task dataset can be supplied, and a candidate is scored by running the agent over it.
- [ ] The reported score comes from a held-out split.
- [ ] The dataset, the scorer, and the permission/sandbox layers are frozen against modification by the search, enforced at the proposal filter.
- [ ] An improved harness appears as a reviewable, versioned proposal and is never self-applied.
- [ ] Reverting to the previous harness is one action.
- [ ] A run states its budget and stops at it.

## Open questions

- Should a run evolve one specialist at a time, or the whole bundle? One at a time attributes wins more cleanly; the whole bundle can find interactions.
- Where does a task dataset live — a repository artifact, a workspace file, or a first-class store object?
- Which engine fits better? PUCT refines one starting point; OpenEvolve's islands keep diversity, which may matter more when a prompt change can be good in one dimension and harmful in another.
- What is the minimum dataset size where a win is believable rather than noise, given the non-determinism the judge mode already documents?
- Should this reuse `/evolve-design`'s checkpointed design conversation, or have its own entry point?

Related: [#50](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/50) — the engines can be started but not observed or stopped from the CLI, which matters more for a search whose evaluations are full agent runs.
items.title: [Feature] RSI — evolve the agent's own harness against a task dataset, reusing the agentdescent search

items.body:
## Summary

Both long-running engines — the evolution search and the Idea Tree — can be **started** from the command line but cannot be **observed, controlled, or stopped** from it. Their progress is designed to land on a frontend card, so a terminal user gets a run id and then nothing. I would like `evolve` and `idea` subcommands that reuse the HTTP endpoints the Web UI already calls.

## What happens today

Starting works. `ScienceDiscovery run "/evolve-design --algorithm puct …"` reaches the same control plane as the browser, the agent loads the `evolve-design` skill, and it calls `create_evolve_run`. Then the turn ends — deliberately. The tool's own result text instructs the model:

> The search runs for minutes to hours and its card streams live progress on its own — do not wait for it here, and do not poll `get_evolve_run`.

`create_idea_research` says the same thing:

> After success, report the handoff and end this turn; the existing tree card streams progress. Do not poll or start another research to wait for completion.

That is the right call for the agent loop — polling would burn the budget the search itself needs. But it means **the card is the only progress surface**, and the CLI has no equivalent. `ScienceDiscovery run` prints `Search created: <uuid>` and exits while the search keeps running server-side for hours.

`services/launcher/src/cli-options.ts` has no evolve or idea-tree subcommand and no related flag. So from a terminal today you cannot:

- list the searches or researches that exist;
- see how far one has got;
- fetch a candidate;
- stop one, or pause and resume it.

The only workaround is starting another `run` in the same session and hoping the model calls `get_evolve_run` / `get_idea_research` — a whole model turn spent reading a status field, using tools whose descriptions explicitly tell the model not to poll them.

## The endpoints already exist

The Web UI drives all of this over plain HTTP:

**Evolve**
- `GET /api/evolve/runs`
- `GET /api/evolve/runs/<id>/events?after=<cursor>`
- `GET /api/evolve/runs/<id>/candidates/<codeHash>`
- `POST /api/evolve/runs/<id>/stop`

**Idea Tree**
- `GET /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/research`
- `POST /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/research` — `pause`, `continue`, `stop`, `defaults`
- `GET /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/research/<rid>/events`
- `GET /api/sessions/<sid>/idea-tree/graph`

## The client plumbing also already exists

`services/launcher/src/control-plane-client.ts` has an authenticated generic `request<T>(path, init)` and `subscribeRunEvents()`, a working SSE consumer that "mirrors the Web frontend's `subscribeRunEvents`: fetch with `accept: text/event-stream`, split frames". The launcher also already resolves the bearer token from the data directory. A `watch` subcommand is that SSE reader pointed at a different path — this is wiring, not new infrastructure.

## Proposal

```
ScienceDiscovery evolve list
ScienceDiscovery evolve get <run-id> [--candidate <hash>]
ScienceDiscovery evolve watch <run-id>
ScienceDiscovery evolve stop <run-id>

ScienceDiscovery idea list --session <id>
ScienceDiscovery idea get <research-id> --session <id>
ScienceDiscovery idea watch <research-id> --session <id>
ScienceDiscovery idea pause|continue|stop <research-id> --session <id>
```

Conventions, matching what `run` already does:

- **text on a TTY, JSONL when piped.** `run` already switches output mode this way; these commands should not invent a second convention.
- **`watch` resumes rather than replays.** The evolve event endpoint already takes `?after=<cursor>`; a dropped connection should continue from the last event seen.
- **Token and data-dir handling identical to `run`** — sharing a `--data-dir` with `serve` should mean no extra configuration.

One asymmetry to decide: evolve exposes only `stop`, while Idea Tree has `pause` / `continue` / `stop`. Either the CLI mirrors each engine's real capabilities, or evolve gains pause/resume — worth an explicit choice rather than an accident.

## Why it matters

- **Unattended and batch use.** Starting a search from a job script is pointless if the same script cannot poll it, stop it when a budget is spent, or collect the winning candidate.
- **Headless and remote machines.** On a workstation reached over SSH there is no browser to hold the card open. Today that machine can start a multi-hour search it cannot then observe.
- **Consistency.** The CLI is already positioned as the scriptable twin of the Web UI; the two most expensive operations in the product are exactly the ones it cannot drive.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Evolve searches and Idea Tree researches can be listed, inspected, watched, and stopped from the CLI.
- [ ] `watch` streams live and resumes from a cursor after a dropped connection.
- [ ] Output follows the existing TTY/pipe convention, so `| jq` works.
- [ ] No new authentication path: the token comes from the data directory as `run` already does.
- [ ] Commands and options appear in `help` and in the CLI reference.
- [ ] Stopping from the CLI has the same effect as stopping from the UI card.

## Open questions

- Should `run` gain an optional `--wait` that blocks until a started engine finishes? Useful in scripts, but these runs last hours — probably better served by `watch`.
- Should `watch` exit non-zero when the run ends in failure, so a script can branch on it?
- Does `evolve list` need session/project scoping, given `GET /api/evolve/runs` is global today?

Related: [#30](https://github.com/openJiuwen-ai/sciencediscovery/issues/30) (introduce the CLI in the README) — that issue is about making the CLI discoverable; this one is about the two workflows it cannot reach.
